tldr: Researchers have developed Tactus, a thin sensing glove integrating 47 capacitive tactile sensors and 16 IMUs into a 3D-knit fabric that preserves natural hand movements while delivering occlusion-resilient contact force and hand pose tracking.
hero_caption: Overall appearance and system configuration of Tactus. It integrates 47 capacitive tactile sensing cells from fingertips to palm and 16 six-axis IMUs distributed across finger phalanges and the hand dorsum, running completely wire-free and self-contained.
overview:
To equip robots with dexterous manipulation skills, high-quality demonstration data of natural human hand movements is essential. However, camera-only egocentric hand tracking easily breaks down the moment hands interact with objects due to heavy occlusions, and it cannot directly measure contact forces. On the other hand, conventional exoskeletons and commercial data gloves dull tactile sensation and restrict joint mobility, distorting natural grasping behaviors.

To solve this dilemma, the authors introduce Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove with a thin 1.5 mm 3D-knit fingertip stackup. It measures contact force and hand pose simultaneously while preserving near-bare-hand natural dexterity. By analyzing empirical contact frequency maps and skin creasing geometry, Tactus optimizes sensor placement across the hand. It also establishes a pneumatic factory calibration routine alongside a simple per-session calibration step to adjust for individual wearers. Furthermore, by fusing egocentric vision with distributed on-glove IMUs, Tactus reliably tracks joint angles even when hands are heavily occluded by manipulated objects.

In real-world evaluations, task completion time while wearing Tactus was just 106% of bare-hand time, significantly outperforming commercial tactile gloves and exoskeletons in naturalness. It achieved a fine minimum detectable force of 0.59 N and sustained an 11.0 mm fingertip relative error under severe occlusion. These signals enable object property estimation, slip detection, and accurate 3D hand-object interaction modeling, providing a solid foundation for contact-aware robot policy and world model learning.
contributions: Developed a thin sensing glove with a 1.5 mm fingertip stackup in a 3D-knit form factor, achieving near-bare-hand task completion time (106% of bare-hand) without disrupting natural grasping behavior.
Optimized tactile sensor layout based on empirical contact frequency and skin deformation geometry, securing 65% fingertip coverage across diverse hand sizes in a single glove size.
Established a practical force calibration pipeline featuring pneumatic-chamber-based uniform batch factory calibration and a simple one-parameter per-session scaling step.
Formulated standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose tracking, conducting the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation against commercial tactile gloves.

sections.heading: Why do we need a new sensing glove now?
sections.summary: High-quality human demonstrations are vital for learning dexterous robotic manipulation, yet vision-only and exoskeleton setups suffer from occlusions or movement restriction. Tactus embeds tactile sensors and IMUs into thin knitwear to capture reliable force and pose data without impairing natural dexterity.
sections.details:
Learning from human demonstrations is a promising path toward human-like robotic dexterity. However, the quality of collected demonstration data directly dictates the performance of the final manipulation policy. Currently, there are three main approaches to capturing human hand movements.

The first approach relies solely on egocentric computer vision (ego-CV). While non-invasive and natural, severe occlusions occur right when hands contact objects—the exact moments where manipulation data is most valuable—causing pose estimation to fail. Some prior works report that less than 10% of raw video data could be used for training. Crucially, vision cannot directly measure contact forces needed for delicate tasks.

The second approach uses exoskeletons. While they offer high kinematic accuracy, their rigid mechanical links restrict range of motion and alter natural grasping strategies. The third approach is sensing gloves, but no wearable platform has combined calibrated force sensing and occlusion-resilient pose tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces Tactus. By integrating 47 capacitive tactile sensing cells and 16 six-axis IMUs into a 3D-knit structure with a 1.5 mm fingertip stackup, Tactus enables simultaneous, high-precision force and pose capture while preserving natural manipulation behavior.

captions.F1: Hardware architecture of Tactus. It connects 47 capacitive tactile cells spanning the fingertips to the palm with 15 finger IMU islands and 1 root IMU on the hand dorsum (16 IMUs in total) via stretchable interconnects.

sections.heading: Evolution and limits of vision, wearables, and pose tracking
sections.summary: Past research explored vision-based force estimation, dense sensor gloves, and sparse IMU tracking. However, uncalibrated signals, tactile blunting, and tracking failures during heavy occlusions remained unresolved.
sections.details:
The authors summarize related prior work along four axes:

- Vision-only contact and force estimation: Prior works infer contact forces through skin blanching or mesh deformation in physics simulations. However, these are indirect inferences and lack calibrated real-world ground truth data.
- Wearables for manipulation data collection: Platforms like STAG (548 sensors across the hand), OSMO (magnetic tracking), and commercial tactile gloves have emerged. Yet they often lack rigorous per-sensor calibration pipelines, and their operational performance during realistic manipulation remains poorly characterized. Exoskeletons, meanwhile, fundamentally alter contact strategies.
- Hand pose tracking during manipulation: Monocular and multi-view vision struggles significantly during hand-object contact, and optical motion capture is vulnerable to marker occlusion. Glove-based approaches using strain gauges or IMUs have faced drift and hysteresis upon donning. Recently, fusing sparse IMUs with vision has gained traction.
- Tactile sensor calibration: Soft, elastic textile gloves deform when worn, altering sensor baselines and sensitivities across postures, making rigorous individual force calibration extremely difficult. While uniform pneumatic calibration has been applied to rigid or planar sensors, adapting it across a full 3D soft glove remained an open challenge.

sections.heading: Three core design pillars and hardware implementation
sections.summary: By co-optimizing thickness, stiffness, and friction, Tactus delivers near-bare-hand natural manipulation. It pairs contact-informed tactile sensor placement with distributed 6-axis IMUs on each phalanx and spring-like stretchable wiring.
sections.details:
To preserve natural human grasping behavior, the design team focused on co-optimizing three physical properties: thickness, stiffness, and friction.

For thickness, pilot tests showed that stackups above 1.5 mm increased completion time and altered grasp choices. Tactus embeds sensors directly into the knit to maintain a 1.5 mm fingertip stackup. For stiffness, it exhibits high compliance with bending stiffness of 0.20 N and tensile stiffness of 0.22 N (per 25 mm width), conforming closely to 3D finger contours. For friction, fingertip TPU coating sets the static coefficient of friction (COF) to 0.4, closely matching bare skin.

### III-A Tactile Sensing Design
The tactile sensors use a two-layer weft-knit capacitive structure, detecting capacitance changes as conductive yarns compress under normal force. Sensor layouts were determined by three empirical datasets:

First, ink-transfer contact frequency heatmaps revealed higher contact frequency on the ulnar side for the thumb and the radial side for the other fingers. Second, kinematic skin creasing and palmar hollow analyses identified dead zones where sensors should be excluded to avoid spurious readings. Third, population coverage analysis showed that keeping sensor width under 50% of finger circumference and fabric modulus around 7 N/cm achieves 65% fingertip coverage across diverse hand sizes with a single glove size. In total, 47 sensing cells are deployed: a 4×2 array on each fingertip, plus discrete cells on phalanges and the palm.

### III-B Pose Tracking Design
To overcome visual occlusions, 16 six-axis IMUs (accelerometer and gyroscope) are distributed across the hand: one on each phalanx and one on the dorsum. Magnetometers were omitted to avoid magnetic interference, and joint orientations are sampled at 200 Hz.

### III-C Supporting Electronics and Interconnects
To prevent wires from restricting finger flexion, stretchable spring-like interconnects (over 70% elongation) were developed by overmolding TPU onto Mylar-wrapped Kevlar-core tinsel wires. Miniaturized island PCBs integrating microcontrollers (PSoC 6) and IMUs communicate with the dorsal controller over UART. A 900 mAh battery enables over 3.5 hours of continuous wireless operation.

captions.F4: Three empirical datasets that guided tactile sensor layout: (A) contact frequency heatmaps identifying high-priority areas, (B) skin crease mapping to exclude fold regions and prevent motion artifacts, and (C) 3D surface scans highlighting non-conformal hollow zones like the palmar arch.

sections.heading: Pneumatic batch calibration and vision-IMU fusion pipeline
sections.summary: A custom pneumatic chamber calibrates all 47 tactile sensors in 23 minutes, while a one-parameter session scaling corrects for individual donning differences. Pose tracking supports three modes: real-time EKF, deep attention fusion, and high-accuracy offline optimization.
sections.details:
Calibration has long been the primary bottleneck for soft tactile gloves. Tactus introduces a two-stage calibration pipeline to resolve this.

### IV-A Tactile Calibration Pipeline
The first stage is factory calibration. A sealed pneumatic chamber with a thermoformed elastic membrane applies uniform air pressure to the glove mounted on an articulated hand form (Hannekin). All 47 sensors undergo 0–15 PSIG pressure cycles simultaneously, fitting a cubic polynomial transfer function $Y = A(X - B)^3 + C$ in under 23 minutes.

The second stage is online per-session calibration. When worn by different users, hand size and skin pre-tension alter sensor gains. The wearer performs a brief fingertip press against a reference load cell, identifying a single scaling parameter $\alpha$ from the ratio between raw and reference readings. This simple step improves median force RMSE by 1.7–2.9×, effectively absorbing donning and subject variability.

### IV-B Hand Pose Tracking Pipeline
Three tracking pipelines were developed to suit different data collection needs:

- EKF Fusion: A real-time mode asynchronously fusing 26-DoF hand pose estimates from an egocentric ResNet with on-glove IMU data.
- AVI-HT (Attention Vision-IMU Hand Tracking): A deep learning framework using hierarchical cross-sensor attention to bind visual features and IMU tokens, maintaining kinematic validity and high accuracy in real time under occlusion.
- Offline Sequence Optimization: A non-linear trajectory optimization leveraging full temporal context across the entire recording to yield the highest kinematic accuracy for imitation learning datasets.

captions.F6: Pneumatic factory calibration rig. A thermoformed bladder uniformly pressurizes the glove mounted on an articulated hand form (Hannekin), calibrating all 47 tactile cells in a single rapid batch.

sections.heading: Standardized benchmark evaluations: naturalness, force, and pose
sections.summary: Using three standardized protocols, Tactus was evaluated against commercial tactile gloves and exoskeletons for natural dexterity, force regression, and pose estimation. Tactus matched bare-hand completion time at 106% and achieved superior minimum detectable force and fingertip tracking accuracy under occlusion.
sections.details:
This work establishes three standardized evaluation protocols to provide fair, objective comparisons across tactile gloves.

### V-A Protocol Dexterous-Tasks (Natural Manipulation)
Participants performed 23 dexterous manipulation tasks spanning ADLs and clinical tests under bare-hand, Tactus, commercial tactile gloves (PPS, JQ), and exoskeleton conditions. Task completion time ratio relative to bare hands was 106% for Tactus, whereas PPS reached 133% and the exoskeleton reached 147%. Tactus also scored the lowest subjective workload on NASA-TLX (2.97), demonstrating minimal interference with natural motion.

### V-B Protocol Tactile (Tactile Accuracy)
Fingertip pressing tasks were benchmarked against a 6-axis force sensor (Nano-17) as ground truth. Tactus achieved a minimum detectable force (MDF) of 0.59 N at 95% confidence—1.6–2.7× lower than PPS (1.61 N) and JQ (0.93 N). It also showed the lowest pose-related artifact ratio (PRA = 0.07) and the highest cross-participant consistency (0.87).

### V-C Protocol Hand Pose (Pose Tracking Accuracy)
Hand pose tracking was evaluated against optical motion capture (OptiTrack) during object manipulation. In wrist-aligned fingertip relative error (f.mkpe.t), AVI-HT reached 11.7 mm and offline optimization reached 11.0 mm, outperforming the vision-only baseline (13.3 mm). The IMUs preserve joint angle observations, preventing tracking collapse during heavy occlusions.

sections.heading: Three downstream tasks powered by tactile and pose fusion
sections.summary: Calibrated tactile feedback paired with occlusion-resilient hand pose enables classifying 9 surface textures, detecting incipient slip with an F1 score of 1.00, and recovering consistent 3D hand-object interactions.
sections.details:
To showcase the utility of Tactus's multimodal signals, the authors validated three downstream manipulation tasks where vision alone falls short.

### VI-A Surface Texture Roughness Estimation
A Transformer model classified 9 distinct texture pads from dynamic tactile signals as fingertips stroked the surfaces. Compared to zero-shot inference from a vision-language model (Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct), the tactile model captured subtle textural differences invisible in camera images, highlighting the value of tactile sensing.

### VI-B Incipient and Gross Slip Detection
A dedicated test rig using a motorized rotary stage and spring generated controlled stick-slip events during fingertip contact. Although Tactus sensors measure normal pressure, spatial redistribution across the sensing array during shear loading allows a temporal convolutional network (CNN) to detect slip onset with an F1 score of 1.00 and an average latency under 0.01 seconds.

### VI-C Hand-Object Interaction Modeling
When manipulating objects like cups, vision-only methods (HaMeR + FoundationPose) lose tracking during finger-object occlusions or two-handed interactions. By combining Tactus's IMU-derived hand pose with kinematic contact constraints from tactile cells, joint trajectory optimization reliably recovers coherent 3D poses for both hands and objects under heavy occlusion.

captions.F8: Comparison of hand-object interaction tracking. Vision-only baselines (HaMeR + FoundationPose) suffer tracking failure or scale collapse during occlusions, whereas integrating Tactus pose and tactile contact constraints reliably recovers consistent 3D hand and object configurations.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: Tactus integrates thin knitwear, data-driven sensor placement, fast pneumatic calibration, and standardized evaluation protocols. Future work will investigate long-term wear durability and further simplify per-session calibration.
sections.details:
This paper presented Tactus, a smart sensing glove that captures calibrated contact forces and occlusion-resilient hand poses while preserving natural human manipulation.

The core contributions include the thin 1.5 mm 3D-knit stackup, contact-frequency-optimized sensor layout, a batch pneumatic calibration pipeline, and standardized benchmarking protocols for fair cross-platform comparison. Key metrics—such as a 0.59 N minimum detectable force, 11.0 mm fingertip tracking error under occlusion, and a 106% task completion time relative to bare hands—highlight its practicality for robot imitation learning and world model data collection.

Future research will focus on scaling user studies across broader participant demographics and diverse objects, streamlining or automating the per-session calibration step, and systematically characterizing viscoelastic fatigue and signal drift over long-term glove lifecycles.

takeaways: Prioritizing minimal sensor thickness (1.5 mm) and low stiffness preserves natural bare-hand grasp strategies and task completion times.
Fusing occlusion-vulnerable vision with drift-prone IMUs provides complementary strengths, dramatically improving hand pose accuracy during critical object grasping phases.
Combining pneumatic batch factory calibration with a simple one-parameter session adjustment enables repeatable, calibrated force measurement on soft textile gloves.
Benchmarking wearable collection systems requires evaluating behavioral naturalness (completion time ratio) and pose-related artifacts (PRA), not just static sensor accuracy.
limitations: Requires an active per-session online calibration step (pressing a reference sensor), which adds operational overhead during large-scale data collection.
Slip detection relies on spatial normal pressure redistribution rather than direct shear force sensing, leaving generalization across diverse preloads and shear directions incompletely verified.
Viscoelastic material fatigue from repeated donning and stretching causes an approximate 3% full-span baseline drop and increased hysteresis across extended sessions.
